chunks: Four witnesses testified against a married man (muhsan) for adultery (zina), then one of them retracted after the man was killed. He said: If the fourth witness says 'I was mistaken', he is to be lashed the legal penalty (hadd) and fined the blood money (diya); but if he says 'I did it deliberately', he is to be killed.

key_terms.أَوْهَمْتُ: Awhamtu — 'I was mistaken/deluded'; implies an unintentional error in testimony
key_terms.الدِّيَةَ: Diya — blood money; the monetary compensation due to the heirs of a wrongfully killed person
key_terms.الزِّنَى: Zina — unlawful sexual intercourse, one of the hudud offenses requiring four witnesses
key_terms.الْحَدَّ: Hadd — the fixed legal punishment prescribed in Islamic law; here, the hadd for qadhf (false accusation of zina) is 80 lashes
key_terms.تَعَمَّدْتُ: Ta'ammadtu — 'I acted deliberately/intentionally'; implies knowing false testimony constituting perjury
key_terms.مُحْصَنٍ: Muhsan — a married person subject to stoning (rajm) rather than lashing as the prescribed punishment for adultery

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic ruling when a witness retracts testimony after an execution for adultery?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) rules on the grave legal consequences when a witness in a capital adultery case retracts his testimony after the convicted man has already been executed. The ruling distinguishes between two scenarios based on the witness's stated intent: if the retraction is due to error, he receives the hadd punishment for false accusation (qadhf) and is liable for the blood money; if the retraction is a deliberate confession of perjury, he faces execution. This ruling reflects the strict Shia jurisprudential principle that false testimony leading to wrongful death makes the witness directly liable for the victim's life.
